newsitem.title: UK: Dlr rallies amid European currency policy tensions.
newsitem.headline: Dlr rallies amid European currency policy tensions.

text.p: The dollar staged a strong rally against the major European currencies here as speculation grew about growing pressure on the leading industrialised nations to allow a general revaluation of the dollar in Europe.

A stream of comments from influential French politicians and central bankers this month all centred around demands for a significantly higher dollar against the franc and other European currencies. The Bundesbank was criticised for not facilitating this rise and devaluation talk circulated in France.
The French and Swiss francs led the way lower against the dollar today to six-month and 21-month lows respectively.

At 1600, the dollar traded at 5.2250/70, up almost three centimes from 5.1995/05 late Thursday and just off highs at 5.2311.Against the Swiss franc, it was 1.3013/23, up from 1.2953/63 yesterday and slightly below today's high at 1.3038.
Dollar/mark rallied as high as 1.5388 - its highest level since October 21 - and clsoed the day near that high at 1.5376/83, up more than half a centime from Thursday.

"Today's market has very much beeen a dollar/Europe play, with dollar gains across the board as the French and German currency debate goes on," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.

There was no specific impetus today to focus on but analysts said there was growing interest in French pressure on Germany to help lift the dollar across the board, and help offset the monetary and fiscal impact of European monetary union.

The French authorities said they do not want to weaken the franc against the mark, lynchpin exchange rate for EMU. But, there is talk that recent comments carry an implicit threat that if Germany does not push for a higher dollar, France may be forced to allow the franc depreciate across the board.
The relative silence from Frankfurt and Bonn on the issue has led some traders to deduce grudging complicity.
Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick was reported late today as welcoming the dollar's rise back above 1.50 marks as good for Germany and German exporters, traders said.
Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet said there was no fundamental reason to devalue the franc against the mark but pointedly did not refer to the dollar exchange rate.

German Finance Minister responded to the French comments - from the likes of former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing and Bank of France council member Jean-Pierre Gerard - by rejecting criticism of the Bundesbank and rubbishing talk of devaluation. But he too made no comment on the dollar.

"In a sense France is holding a loaded gun to Germany's head saying either we revalue mark/Paris or Europe as a block devalues against the U.S. and the rest of the world," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Traders will be keep a close eye on any news or comment surrounding the informal meeting between German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac tomorrow in the southwestern French town of Perigueux on Saturday.
However, analysts said the heightened currency debate internally in France may be exaggerated by the release Monday of the French October unemployment rate, which is expected to rise.
Analysts polled by Reuters expect the French jobless rate to rise to 12.7 percent in October from 12.6 percent.
Other major calendar dates to watch will be the December 13 and 14 EU summit and the next meeting of the finance minsters of the Group of Seven industrialised nations early next year.

Some analysts, however, believe the French authorities may have been happy to allow the devaluation threat to come out in the open to counter-balance Germany's behind-the-scenes threat to delay EMU if the rest of Europe does not concede to its stict post-EMU budget stability pact.
